\chapter{Saying When}
\label{ch:ml-when}
\hlchaptermodality{102}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say that something happens on a named day or at a named hour, and ask what time it happens.}

From cold: two answers to \textquotedblleft{}when\textquotedblright{}, and which of the two takes an ending.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[raṇṭŭ maṇikkŭ]{\ml{രണ്ട്} \ml{മണിക്ക്} — at two o'clock}

\label{lesson:ML-C102-manikku}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{two o'clock}. Then say the ending chapter 6 gave you for \textbf{to} and \textbf{for}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\textbf{\ml{രണ്ട്} \ml{മണി}} \emph{names} an hour. Add the dative and you are no longer naming it — you are putting something \textbf{at} it.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ml{രണ്ട്} \ml{മണി}} & \emph{raṇṭŭ maṇi} & two o'clock \\
\textbf{\ml{രണ്ട്} \ml{മണിക്ക്}} & \emph{raṇṭŭ maṇikkŭ} & at two o'clock \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{Nothing about the ending is new.} You built this exact landing in chapter 6: \textbf{\ml{ജോലി}} ends in \textbf{\ml{ി}}, so it took \textbf{\ml{ക്ക്}} and gave \textbf{\ml{ജോലിക്ക്}}. \textbf{\ml{മണി}} ends in that same letter and takes that same ending, with the same visible seam — \textbf{\ml{മണി}} plus \textbf{\ml{ക്ക്}}.

\begin{culture}
Chapter 6 glossed this ending \textbf{to} and \textbf{for}, and English will not accept either one here: \emph{to two o'clock} is not a thing anybody says. English reaches for a third word, \textbf{at}.

\textbf{That is a fact about English, not about the ending.} Malayalam has not switched cases on you — the suffix on \textbf{\ml{മണിക്ക്}} is letter for letter the one you put on \textbf{\ml{ജോലി}}. What has changed is the English word you need to translate it, and English has three of them where Malayalam has one ending. When you meet this ending on an hour, read it \textbf{at}.
\end{culture}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the slot at the front}]
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ml{രണ്ട്} \ml{മണിക്ക്} \ml{ഞാൻ} \ml{പോകും}.} — \emph{raṇṭŭ maṇikkŭ ñān pōkuṁ} — \textquotedblleft{}At two o'clock I will go.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

You know that sentence already. Chapter 94 stood \textbf{\ml{ഇന്ന്}} at the front of it, and \textbf{\ml{നാളെ}}, and told you the verb at the back is what carries the tense. The front is a slot for saying \textbf{when}.

What is new is the toll. \textbf{\ml{ഇന്ന്}} walked into that slot wearing nothing. An hour has to put an ending on before it is allowed in.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{raṇṭŭ maṇi} — naming the hour
  \item \emph{raṇṭŭ maṇikkŭ} — putting something at it
  \item \emph{raṇṭŭ maṇikkŭ ñān pōkuṁ}
  \item which chapter you first built this ending on, and on which word
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is the difference between \textbf{\ml{രണ്ട്} \ml{മണി}} and \textbf{\ml{രണ്ട്} \ml{മണിക്ക്}}? (\textbf{The first names the hour; the second puts something at it}.) Which ending did you add? (\textbf{\ml{ക്ക്}} — the dative from chapter 6.) Why does English need a different word here than it did for \emph{to me}? (\textbf{English splits the job across to, for and at; Malayalam does not}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[thiṅkaḷāzhcha ñān pōkuṁ]{\ml{തിങ്കളാഴ്ച} \ml{ഞാൻ} \ml{പോകും} — on Monday I will go}

\label{lesson:ML-C102-azhcha}



\begin{quote}
Say the day-name for Monday. Then say \emph{at two o'clock}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
Chapter 10 laid the seven day-names out in a table and left them there. You have read \textbf{\ml{തിങ്കളാഴ്ച}} and never once \emph{used} it. Use it now:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ml{തിങ്കളാഴ്ച} \ml{ഞാൻ} \ml{പോകും}.} — \emph{thiṅkaḷāzhcha ñān pōkuṁ} — \textquotedblleft{}On Monday I will go.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\textbf{Read that sentence twice and look for the ending.} There is none. The day-name went into the when-slot exactly as it stands in chapter 10's table, with nothing added to the front of it and nothing added to the back.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: two words, one slot, one ending between them}]
Put the last lesson's sentence beside this one and the difference is the whole point of the chapter:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ml{രണ്ട്} \ml{മണിക്ക്} \ml{ഞാൻ} \ml{പോകും}} & \emph{raṇṭŭ maṇikkŭ…} & the hour took \textbf{\ml{ക്ക്}} \\
\textbf{\ml{തിങ്കളാഴ്ച} \ml{ഞാൻ} \ml{പോകും}} & \emph{thiṅkaḷāzhcha…} & the day took \textbf{nothing} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Both sentences answer \textbf{when}. Both put their answer at the front. One of the two answers had to put an ending on first, and it is the hour.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{culture}
\textbf{The day-name is in good company.} \textbf{\ml{ഇന്ന്}} and \textbf{\ml{നാളെ}} stand in that same slot bare, and they have since chapter 94. A named day behaves like \emph{today} and \emph{tomorrow}, not like a clock time.

So the line you can rely on, for what this book has taught you, runs between \textbf{the named day} and \textbf{the named hour} — and it is the hour that is the odd one. That is a description of what Malayalam does here, not a law with no exceptions: a day-name can take endings for other jobs. For saying \textbf{when} something happens, it does not need one.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{thiṅkaḷāzhcha}
  \item \emph{thiṅkaḷāzhcha ñān pōkuṁ}
  \item \emph{raṇṭŭ maṇikkŭ ñān pōkuṁ}, then the Monday line again
  \item which of the two answers carried an ending, and which carried none
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What do you add to \textbf{\ml{തിങ്കളാഴ്ച}} to say \emph{on Monday}? (\textbf{Nothing}.) What do you add to \textbf{\ml{രണ്ട്} \ml{മണി}} to say \emph{at two}? (\textbf{\ml{ക്ക്}}.) Which two words from chapter 94 stand in that slot bare, the way the day-name does? (\textbf{\ml{ഇന്ന്}} and \textbf{\ml{നാളെ}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ethra maṇikkŭ]{\ml{എത്ര} \ml{മണിക്ക്} — at what time?}

\label{lesson:ML-C102-ethra-manikku}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{how far}. Say \emph{how much}. Then say \emph{at two o'clock}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\textbf{\ml{എത്ര}} is not new. It asked \emph{how old} in chapter 19, \emph{how far} in chapter 81 and \emph{how much} in chapter 91. Two of those three are built the way you need here — \textbf{\ml{എത്ര}}, then the thing you want measured:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ml{എത്ര} \ml{ദൂരം}} & \emph{ethra dūraṁ} & how far? \\
\textbf{\ml{എത്ര} \ml{രൂപ}} & \emph{ethra rūpa} & how much? \\
\textbf{\ml{എത്ര} \ml{മണിക്ക്}} & \emph{ethra maṇikkŭ} & at what time? \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Put a hand over the question word and what is left is a distance, a price, and an hour.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: which word wears the ending}]
In \emph{how far} and \emph{how much} the noun stands bare. In \textbf{\ml{എത്ര} \ml{മണിക്ക്}} it carries \textbf{\ml{ക്ക്}}. \textbf{\ml{എത്ര}} itself is identical in all three — the ending belongs to the hour, not to the question.

And the answer gives it back:

\begin{quote}
— \textbf{\ml{എത്ര} \ml{മണിക്ക്}?} — \emph{ethra maṇikkŭ?} — \textbf{\ml{രണ്ട്} \ml{മണിക്ക്}.} — \emph{raṇṭŭ maṇikkŭ.}
\end{quote}
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{culture}
\textbf{The ending is doing some of the asking.} Drop it and the question changes: \textbf{\ml{എത്ര} \ml{മണി}} asks somebody to \emph{name} the hour, and \textbf{\ml{എത്ര} \ml{മണിക്ക്}} asks at which hour a thing will happen.

The day-name has no such pair, because it never took the ending at all.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{ethra dūraṁ}, \emph{ethra rūpa}, \emph{ethra maṇikkŭ}
  \item the question, then answer it — \emph{ethra maṇikkŭ? raṇṭŭ maṇikkŭ.}
  \item \emph{ethra maṇi?}, then \emph{ethra maṇikkŭ?} — and name the difference
  \item which word in the question carries the ending, and which does not
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How do you ask \emph{at what time?} (\textbf{\ml{എത്ര} \ml{മണിക്ക്}}.) Which of the two words carries the ending? (\textbf{\ml{മണി}} — the question word never changes.) What does the answer wear? (\textbf{The same ending} — \ml{രണ്ട്} \ml{മണിക്ക്}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[thiṅkaḷāzhcha raṇṭŭ maṇikkŭ]{\ml{തിങ്കളാഴ്ച} \ml{രണ്ട്} \ml{മണിക്ക്} — on Monday at two o'clock}

\label{lesson:ML-C102-day-and-hour}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{on Monday}. Say \emph{at two o'clock}. Now say them one after the other, without stopping.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
You have two answers to \textbf{when}, and real arrangements usually need both:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ml{തിങ്കളാഴ്ച} \ml{രണ്ട്} \ml{മണിക്ക്} \ml{ഞാൻ} \ml{പോകും}.} \emph{thiṅkaḷāzhcha raṇṭŭ maṇikkŭ ñān pōkuṁ} \textquotedblleft{}On Monday at two o'clock I will go.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\textbf{Neither piece changed to make room for the other.} The day-name is the bare word from chapter 10. The hour is the dative you built two lessons ago. They stand side by side in the one slot at the front, and the sentence behind them is untouched.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: wider first}]
The order is not free, and it is the order you would guess: \textbf{the wider container goes first.} A Monday holds a two o'clock; a two o'clock does not hold a Monday.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
day, then hour & \textbf{\ml{തിങ്കളാഴ്ച} \ml{രണ്ട്} \ml{മണിക്ക്}} \\
what English does & \emph{on Monday at two} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

English arranges it the same way, which here is a genuine convenience rather than a trap — you can carry your instinct straight across.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Count what this chapter actually added: \textbf{one ending, on one kind of word.}

Everything else was already yours — the hour from chapter 18, the day-names from chapter 10, the question word since chapter 19, the slot at the front from chapter 94. What was missing was never vocabulary. It was the joint, and the joint is \textbf{\ml{ക്ക്}} on the hour and nothing at all on the day.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{thiṅkaḷāzhcha raṇṭŭ maṇikkŭ}
  \item the whole sentence — \emph{…ñān pōkuṁ}
  \item \emph{ethra maṇikkŭ?} and answer it with the hour from that sentence
  \item which of the two front words carries an ending, and why the other does not
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which comes first, the day or the hour? (\textbf{The day} — the wider one.) Which of the two carries an ending? (\textbf{The hour}.) What did this chapter add that you did not already own? (\textbf{One ending on one kind of word} — the rest was already yours.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ethra maṇikkŭ enna ōrmma]{(on Monday, at two o'clock, at what time?) — from cold}

\label{lesson:ML-R102-when-recall}



\begin{quote}
Close the lessons before this one. Say \emph{on Monday}, \emph{at two o'clock}, and \emph{at what time?}
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: one of them takes an ending}]
Two answers to the same question, and only one of them is dressed:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ml{തിങ്കളാഴ്ച}} & \emph{thiṅkaḷāzhcha} & on Monday — \textbf{bare} \\
\textbf{\ml{രണ്ട്} \ml{മണിക്ക്}} & \emph{raṇṭŭ maṇikkŭ} & at two o'clock — \textbf{\ml{ക്ക്}} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

If you can remember which one is which, you have the chapter. The day-name stands in the when-slot the way \textbf{\ml{ഇന്ന്}} and \textbf{\ml{നാളെ}} have stood there since chapter 94. The hour does not; it takes the dative first.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
\textbf{No word in this chapter was new.} That is unusual enough to say out loud. The hour came from chapter 18, the day-names from chapter 10, the question word you have used since chapter 19, and the ending itself from chapter 6, where it meant \emph{to} and \emph{for} and landed on \textbf{\ml{ജോലി}} exactly as it now lands on \textbf{\ml{മണി}}.

What you could not do before was \textbf{fix an arrangement in time} — and what was missing was one joint, not a vocabulary list.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{thiṅkaḷāzhcha}, then \emph{raṇṭŭ maṇikkŭ}
  \item \emph{ethra maṇikkŭ?} and answer it
  \item \emph{thiṅkaḷāzhcha raṇṭŭ maṇikkŭ ñān pōkuṁ}
  \item the two words from chapter 94 that behave like the day-name
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
\emph{On Monday}? (\textbf{\ml{തിങ്കളാഴ്ച}} — nothing added.) \emph{At two o'clock}? (\textbf{\ml{രണ്ട്} \ml{മണിക്ക്}}.) \emph{At what time?} (\textbf{\ml{എത്ര} \ml{മണിക്ക്}}.) Which comes first when you say both? (\textbf{The day}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
